strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation of prior NeRF-weight-processing frameworks (nf2vec, Cardace et al.), namely their restriction to a single fixed input architecture; to my knowledge this is the first work to demonstrate a single encoder that ingests both MLP and tri-planar NeRFs and generalizes to architectures unseen at training.

The empirical observation that a rendering loss alone yields architecture-specific clusters, and that a SigLIP contrastive term aligns embeddings of the same object across parameterizations, is a clean and well-supported finding (t-SNE plots plus instance-level retrieval, where LR gets ~0% R@1 and LC ~29%, make the point convincingly).

Careful and informative analysis of the complementary roles of the two losses: LR favors class separability, LC favors architecture invariance, and the classification/retrieval tables consistently reflect this trade-off.

Generalization experiments to six unseen architecture variants (depth, width, grid resolution, channel count) are a meaningful stress test, and the appendix t-SNE on unseen MLPs supports the claim that contrastive training extrapolates invariance beyond the trained architectures.
Writing is clear, method description is precise, and implementation/training details (hyper-parameters, hardware, codebases) are sufficient for reproduction.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the method is an off-the-shelf GMN encoder (Lim et al., 2024, including their graph construction) plugged into the nf2vec encoder-decoder pipeline, plus a standard SigLIP loss. No new architectural, theoretical, or optimization contribution is made, and no GMN-side adaptation specific to NeRFs (e.g. handling large tri-plane grids) is proposed or analyzed.

Key baselines are missing. There is no rendering-based baseline (render k views and classify with a standard image encoder), which is the obvious alternative the introduction dismisses but never quantifies. There is also no comparison against the other GMN formulation (Kofinas et al., 2024), no simple weight-vector baselines (e.g. zero-padding/statistics + MLP), and no attempt to adapt nf2vec/Cardace et al. to the multi-architecture setting (e.g. two separate encoders with a shared head), so the headline multi-architecture tables contain only the authors' own variants and consist entirely of dashes for prior work.

Gains in the single-architecture setting are marginal (93.6 vs 92.1 on MLP; 94.0 vs 93.1 on TRI) and reported without seeds, variance, or significance, so the claim of 'matching or exceeding' prior work rests on within-noise differences.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: a single synthetic dataset (ShapeNetRender), two training architectures, and only classification and retrieval. nf2vec also demonstrates segmentation, generation and completion; none of these are attempted, so it is unclear whether the learned embeddings are generally useful. The authors themselves note that neither considered architecture is state-of-the-art (no hash-grid/Instant-NGP NeRFs), which undercuts the 'Embed Any NeRF' claim.

Robustness to unseen architectures is in fact quite brittle in places (e.g. TRI-8C drops to 11-21% for contrastive variants, TRI-16W to 30% for LR), close to or below chance in some cells; these failures are noted anecdotally but not diagnosed, and no mitigation (e.g. architecture augmentation during training) is explored.

Instance-level retrieval performance is weak in absolute terms (29% R@1 on BOTH), and the paper offers qualitative excuses rather than analysis of why cross-architecture instance identity is not recovered.

Efficiency and scalability are not analyzed despite being central to the motivation: training takes ~2 weeks on a single GPU, and the parameter-graph for a tri-plane grows quickly with resolution/channels. No inference-time comparison against rendering-based pipelines or against nf2vec/Cardace et al. is provided.

Ablations are thin: only three loss configurations, a single fixed lambda chosen by magnitude matching without a sensitivity study, and no ablation on graph features, pooling, or embedding dimension. The choice of SigLIP over InfoNCE is asserted rather than tested.
t-SNE figures show only 6 of the 13 dataset classes without explanation, which weakens the latent-space claims.
